metadata.title: Reading literacy decline in Europe: Disentangling school closures and out-of-school learning conditions during the COVID-19 pandemic

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2016 and PIRLS 2021 student, parent, and school principal data from 18 European countries/regions, restricting to the same test language and a comparable testing window (March–June) and excluding Malta. For trend estimation of out-of-school learning conditions, the authors apply PIRLS student sampling weights and use the R package BIFIE.survey, with standard errors computed via jackknife replication. For the adjusted reading literacy trend (RQ2), they implement propensity score weighting (inverse probability of being a 2021 student) using a logistic regression propensity model and then multiply the resulting IPTW weights (trimmed at the 99th percentile) by the PIRLS sampling weight (SENWGT), thereby combining survey weighting with reweighting for compositional change. The analysis also relies on plausible values for the out-of-school constructs and reading literacy, so weighting is applied within the plausible-value framework rather than as a simple unweighted mean.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample uses PIRLS 2016 and PIRLS 2021 data from 18 European countries/regions, restricted to students with a testing period between March and June in both years and using the same test language (excluding Malta). The study includes representative samples of about 5,000 students per year and country/region, and it reports that the average exclusion rate prior to sampling was equal across 2016 and 2021. For missing data, the authors use a plausible value procedure for the out-of-school learning condition constructs: they calibrate international item parameters with a multi-group generalized partial credit model in TAM and then draw five plausible variables per country and year, imputing missing responses conditional on other variables (functioning like multiple imputation). They also exclude specific out-of-school variables for specific countries when extreme distributional changes were detected between 2016 and 2021 (e.g., ECEC enrollment under three in Denmark and Belgium (fr.), and owning a desk in Italy).

main_findings.target_variable: Reading literacy decline (Cohen's d, observed vs adjusted)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Observed decline: d = −0.16 (se = 0.01, p < .001). Adjusted decline: d = −0.11 (se = 0.01, p < .001). Difference (adjusted − observed): Δadj−obs = +0.05 (reported via Table 1 as adjusted being less negative).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 & 2021 Grade 4 reading literacy data (Europe composite), the study leveraged school-entry reading skills, ECEC enrolment, speaking the test language at home, printed books at home, and parents who like reading to estimate an adjusted reading literacy decline via propensity score weighting. It found that the observed decline (d = −0.16) was partially explained by changes in out-of-school learning conditions, with the adjusted decline reduced to d = −0.11. This indicates that policies addressing students’ out-of-school learning environments (e.g., language support, access to books, and family reading engagement) can mitigate pandemic-era learning losses, even though school closures remain a key driver.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 & 2021 Grade 4 Reading literacy (18 European countries/regions)
main_findings.target_variable: Association between school-closure duration and adjusted reading literacy decline (meta-regression slope)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Meta-regression (adjusted trend): intercept B0 = 0.0018 (se = 0.05, p = .973), slope B1 = −0.0015 (se = 0.0006, p = .014), R2 = .29. Unadjusted (observed trend): intercept B0 = −0.1062 (se = 0.0535, p = .047), slope B1 = −0.0007 (se = 0.0006, p = .285), R2 = .02. Table 2 reports N = 18 countries/regions.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 & 2021 Grade 4 reading literacy data across 18 European countries/regions, the study leveraged out-of-school learning conditions (captured through the six constructs used for propensity score adjustment) to compute adjusted reading literacy declines and then regressed these declines on UNESCO school-closure days. It found a statistically significant negative association for the adjusted trend, with reading literacy declining by −0.0015 SDs per day of COVID-related school closure (p = .014), while the unadjusted slope was not significant. This indicates that longer school closures are linked to greater learning loss even after accounting for compositional changes in out-of-school learning conditions, supporting policy prioritization of minimizing closure duration and implementing large-scale remediation when closures occur.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2016 and PIRLS 2021 Grade 4 reading literacy across 18 European countries/regions (N = 187,386 students), using PIRLS plausible values for reading literacy and for six out-of-school learning condition constructs. It first documents changes in out-of-school conditions between cohorts (e.g., increases in ECEC participation and school-entry reading skills, and decreases in language of instruction at home, parental reading engagement, printed books, and essential learning conditions). For the adjusted trend (RQ2), it applies propensity score weighting to balance out-of-school learning conditions between 2016 and 2021 and finds the average reading literacy decline reduced from d = −0.16 (observed) to d = −0.11 (adjusted), remaining statistically significant. For the closure-duration association (RQ3), meta-regression shows that the adjusted decline is significantly related to school-closure days, at −0.0015 SDs per day (p = .014), with R2 = .29. Limitations include reliance on observational reweighting (not causal identification) and incomplete coverage of some parental background and remote-learning quality measures.
